children: Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman shared on Thursday some early lessons from the bank regulators' revamp of the enhanced supplementary leverage (eSLR) ratio, a capital requirement intended to operate as a backstop to risk-based capital requirements in the U.S.
The eSLR is only applied to the largest banks, called global systemically important banks (GSIBs), and their subsidiaries.

"The impact of this recalibration has been encouraging. So far this year, evidence shows that leverage ratio reforms have improved Treasury market functioning and strengthened its resilience to stress by relaxing regulatory balance sheet constraints," Bowman said in a speech at the Atlantic Council 2026 CEO and Senior Management Summit.

Under the original framework, "the eSLR often became a binding constraint rather than operating as a backstop," she said. "When it is binding or could approach binding, the eSLR distorts incentives and activities."

That resulted in banks pulling back from lower-risk, lower-return activities — such as intermediating the U.S. Treasury market — and instead pursuing higher-risk activities that held the potential for higher returns without corresponding increases in capital requirements.

The misaligned incentives resulted in inefficient capital allocation throughout the financial system, she said. Ultimately, the original framework undermined the market stability it was designed to protect.

"In particular, when banks are constrained by the eSLR ratios, they tended to hold smaller Treasury positions, hampering market liquidity as trading decreased and dealer intermediation margins increased," she said. "In addition, following shocks to the size of bank balance sheets, the reduction in Treasury market participation was larger for banks with lower SLRs."

In November 2025, the Fed, along with the FDIC and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, finalized changes to the eSLR. The change recalibrated the buffer standard for GSIBs to equal 50% of a GSIB's method-1 surcharge calculated under the Board's GSIB surcharge framework, rather than the previous leverage buffer standard of 2%.
After the recalibration, the Fed's supervisory data showed that dealers increased their Treasury market positions, as all the largest banks benefited from greater headroom.

Supervisory data showed that dealers' total Treasury positions increased from roughly $600B at the beginning of the modification period to over $700B at the end of April. The increase was concentrated among the firms that had consistently maintained the lowest eSLR buffers over the previous 24 months and were thus more constrained by the eSLR. "This pattern suggests that the sharp increase in positions was driven by dealers taking advantage of additional headroom created by the eSLR modification," she said.
That has translated into greater balance sheet capacity at dealer subsidiaries, Bowman added.

The Fed is seeing improved market liquidity and functioning across relevant markets through narrower bid-ask spreads, reduced intraday volatility during auction cycles, calmer funding conditions, and greater price stability during periods of elevated supply. "All of this indicates that dealer intermediation is successfully absorbing flows that could have previously caused more pronounced market dislocations," she said.

"Regulations should adapt as conditions evolve and as we gain experience with how rules operate in practice," Bowman  said in her conclusion. "When evidence shows that a regulation is creating adverse unintended consequences, we have a responsibility to act. The eSLR experience demonstrates that thoughtful recalibration — grounded in sound analysis and market feedback — can meaningfully improve both market resilience and the efficiency of our regulatory framework."

Regarding monetary policy, "I don't currently see an urgent need for further action" after the Federal Open Market Committee hiked its benchmark rate by 25 basis points in September. "Inflation remains above our target. What we need is to have a better understanding of trends" in the economy and how the September rate increase flows into the economy, Bowman said.
The Federal Reserve is aiming to finalize the Basel III endgame rules by the end of the year.

title: Fed's Bowman is seeing improved market liquidity from eSLR recalibration for the biggest banks
